Abu Asad Bhuiyan and others ----- Appellants
Vs.

case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated November 2000 passed by the High Court in Civil Revision No. 1434 of 1999)
full_judgment:
Md. Ruhul Amin J: This is defendants appeal by leave against the judgment dated November 5, 2000 of a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1434 of 1999 discharging the Rule obtained against the judgment and decree dated March 24, 1999 of the 2nd Court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Narsingdi in Title Appeal No. 6 of 1998 dismissing the same upon affirming the judgment and decree dated January 22, 1998 of the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Monohardi, Narsingdi in Title Suit No. 64 of 1996 decreeing the same against the defendant Nos. 1-9 on contest and ex parte against the rest declaring the title of the plaintiffs in respect of the land in suit and that the record of rights, i.e. SA and RS khatians, prepared in the name of defendants' predecessor Abu Sufian was wrong.

2. The suit was filed stating, inter alia, that Jagadish Chandra and Ramesh Chandra permanently made settlement of the land in suit to Firoz Bhuiyan, predecessor of the plaintiffs and defendant No. 10 by the Hukumnama dated 10th Kartick, 1344 BS and father of the defendant Nos. 1-9, Abu Sufian put his signature on the Hukumnama as a witness, that Abu Sufian was a clever man and though was not ever the owner and possessor of the land in suit, yet in collusion with the survey officials, managed to get his name recorded in the SA khatian in respect of half of the land taken settlement by Firoz Bhuiyan, that at the time of preparation of the RS record defendant Nos. 1-9's predecessor also got the record of right prepared in his name in respect of 8 annas share on the basis of SA record, that on the basis of the record of right, particularly on the basis of RS record, defendants raised claim in respect of the land taken settlement by Firoz Bhuiyan and that in that state of the matter plaintiffs upon obtaining the copy of the SA and RS record came to know about the preparation of the said records in respect of the land in suit wrongly in the name of the defendant Nos. 1-9 predecessor Hence the suit for declaration of title simplicities.

3. The suit was contested by the defendant Nos. 1-9 by filing written statement denying the material averments made in the plaint and stating, inter alia, that Firoz Bhuiyan and Abu Sufian were full brothers and they used to live jointly, that Firoz Bhuiyan used to look after financial transaction of the family, that the land in suit was settled in the name of the two brothers and the settlement was taken out of the income of the joint family, that Fi n Bhuiyan was entrusted to take settlement in the name of the two brothers but he took the Hukumnama in his name alone, that on the direction of Firoz Bhuiyan SA record was prepared in the name of Firoz Bhuiyan and Abu Sufian each having 8 annas share as regard the land taken settlement by the Hukumnama dated 10th Kartick, 1344 BS as well as paternal land and that in the background of the possession of Abu Sufian RS record was prepared in his name and was published finally in the name of the two brothers recording equal share i.e. 8 annas share each, that SA and RS records were prepared correctly and that the defendants being in possession of the land in suit, the suit framed is not maintainable.

4. The trial Court decreed the suit on the findings that the suit is not barred by limitation, there was no basis for the preparation of SA and RS record in the name of Abu Sufian, that at the time of preparation of the RS record Firoz Bhuiyan was dead and his son Babul was minor, that settlement was given to Firoz Bhuiyan and, as such, Abu Sufian had no right and title in the land in suit, that plaintiffs are in possession of the land in suit, that the defendants failed to establish their claim of being in possession of half of the land recorded in the name of their predecessor.

5. The defendants went on appeal. The appellate Court dismissed the appeal on the finding that from the defendants' side the validity of the Hukumnama has not been challenged and as the Hukumnama is in the name of Firoz Bhuiyan alone, as such, title in the land in suit is of Firoz Bhuiyan, that the allegation of the defendants that Firoz being a clever man beyond the knowledge of Abu Sufian obtained the Hukumnama in his name, if accepted for argument's sake, then signature of Abu Sufian would not have been in the Hukumnama, that there is no explanation from the defendants' side why their predecessor, who is an educated man attested the Hukumnama without taking exception that the Hukumnama was in the name of Firoz Bhuiyan alone, that as Firoz Bhuiyan was dead and his son Babul was minor and because of that RS record was prepared in the name of the plaintiffs and the defendants, that plaintiffs by documentary as well as by oral evidence have established their title and possession in the land in suit. Thereupon, the defendants moved the High Court Division in Revisional jurisdiction and obtained Rule.

6. It was contended before the High Court Division that the suit as framed, i.e. Suit for mere declaration of title alone, is not maintainable since plaintiffs are not in exclusive possession of the land in suit and, as such, they were required to ask for consequential relief and having had not done so the suit was barred by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, that in view of the evidence on record the courts below were required to hold that the defendants are in possession of the land in suit.

7. The High Court Division, while making the Rule absolute in the background of the submission of the learned Counsel for the defendant-petitioners that PW 2 and PW 4. having had admitted possession of the defendants in the land in suit and consequent thereupon suit framed being hit by the provision of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act for not seeking consequential relief the same was not maintainable observed, "in my view, both the plaintiffs and the defendants are in possession and title being in favour of Firoz alone the possession should be construed the possession of Firoz alone and Abu Sufian may be treated as intruder". The High Court Division has also observed that because of the provision of section 91 of the Evidence Act and that as Abu Sufian, predecessor of the defendant-petitioners, attested the Hukumnama as such by the oral evidence defendants are not competent to establish anything contrary to the facts as being reflected by the Hukumnama or in other words defendant-petitioners cannot be allowed to lead evidence to prove something which is otherwise than in the Hukumnama and thereupon, finally observed, "Since the Hukumnama shows that Firoz is the only recipient of the land, oral evidence to prove that the same is not correct cannot be allowed". The High Court Division finally, held that the matters involved in the case are concluded by the concurrent finding of the courts below.

8. Leave was obtained for consideration of the contentions that PW 2 having had stated in his deposition that the suit land has been recorded in the name of Firoz Bhuiyan and Abu Sufian and both of them are in possession and the PW 4 having had stated that Firoz Bhuiyan and Abu Sufian lived in the same homestead and the DWs also having had stated that Firoz and Abu Sufian are in possession of their respective shares, the High Court Division was in error in rejecting the contention of the defendants that they being in possession with the plaintiffs of the land in suit, the suit for mere declaration of title is barred by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and that wrongly arrived at the finding of possession in favour of Firoz alone upon holding possession of Abu Sufian "may be treated as intruder", which is inconsistent to the evidence on record and thus the High Court Division ought to have held that the Courts below committed error of law in not holding that the suit of the plaintiffs was barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, that Courts below misread the evidence, particularly evidence of PWs 2 and 4 along with the evidence of DWs as regard the matter of possession of Abu Sufian and Firoz Bhuiyan and, as such, High Court Division was in error in not holding that the judgment of the courts below are not sustainable being based on misreading of the evidence.

9. The learned Counsel for the appellant has submitted that .the defendants took the plea in their written statement that the suit is barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and that it was specifically pleaded by the defendants that the land in suit is being enjoyed in equal share by the plaintiffs and the defendants and that as the plaintiffs have no exclusive title and possession in the land in suit the plaintiffs cannot have the relief in the suit in the absence of payment of ad valorem court fee.

10. It has been submitted by in the learned Counsel for the appellants that it Was the specific case of the defendants that plaintiffs are not in exclusive possession of the land in suit and that the defendants along with the plaintiffs are in possession of the land in suit. The learned Counsel to substantiate his aforesaid submission has referred to the evidence of PW 1 who has stated that RS record has been prepared wrongly and that on the basis of the wrong record of right defendants for the last one year are in possession of the land in suit. The learned Counsel has also referred to the evidence of PW 2 who has stated in-chief that Firoz Bhuiyan possessed the land in suit exclusively by erecting huts and defendants have no hut. in the land in suit, but in cross-examination the witness has stated it is not known to him whether Abu Sufian's heirs possess 8 annas share of the land in suit. The witness has also stated that persons who have land by the side of the land in suit have not come to depose in the case and that he has no land by the side of the land in suit. The learned Counsel also referred to the evidence of PW 3 who in his deposition has stated that defendants have 3/4 huts in plot No. 777. It may be mentioned in the schedule attached to the plaint plot number of the land in suit has been mentioned as plot No. 777 comprising 1.04 acres of land and out of that 54 decimals of land is the land in suit. PW 4 in his evidence has stated that defendants have 4 huts in the land in suit and PW 5 has stated that his house is by the side of land in suit, that he has heard Firoz Bhuiyan took settlement of the land in his name, that the plaintiffs and defendants are possessing the land in suit. At that stage he was declared hostile and while he was being cross-examined by the plaintiffs the witness denied the suggestion that being gained over by the defendants he has deposed falsely. In cross-examination by the defendants the witness has stated that he has heard plaintiffs and defendants have their huts in the land in suit. The learned Counsel has also referred to the evidence of DWs. DW 1 has stated upon erecting but Abu Sufian possessed the land since 1344 BS and that the SA and RS records were prepared correctly, that Abu Sufian's possession and enjoyment of half of the land was never objected to by Firoz Bhuiyan or by the plaintiffs. DW 2 has stated that plaintiffs and defendants are possessing the land in equal share and DW 4 has stated that Firoz Bhuiyan and Abu Sufian possessed the land in equal share and that defendants are living in the land in suit.

11. In the background of the evidence as referred to above, it was submitted by the learned Counsel of the appellants the suit as framed i.e. seeking simple declaration of title, was not maintainable in view of the provision of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act.

12. The learned Counsel has submitted that although Hukumnama was in the name of Firoz Bhuiyan but from the facts on record it is seen that settlement was taken for the benefit of both the brothers i.e. Firoz Bhuiyan and Abu Sufian who were living jointly and that settlement was taken with the income of joint family. It may be mentioned that the contention as to taking settlement with the income of the joint family has not been established from the side of the defendants. It has also been submitted since Firoz Bhuiyan allowed his brother Abu Sufian to possess half of the land taken settlement by the Hukumnama and during Firoz Bhuiyan's lifetime Abu Sufian constructed huts in half of the land taken settlement and was hying there and that as during Firoz Bhuiyan's lifetime SA record was prepared in the name of Firoz Bhuiyan and Abu Sufian recording 8 arenas share each and as no exception was taken about the preparation of the SA record by Firoz Bhuiyan, the entirety of the facts mentioned hereinbefore thus clearly show that settlement was taken the benefit of Firoz Bhuiyan and Abu Sufian. It is also the contention of the learned Counsel for the appellants that as exception was not taken in respect of the SA record, preparation of the RS record in the light of the SA record in the name of Firoz Bhuiyan and Abu Sufian noting equal share in the land listed in RS khatian cannot be considered wrong, that evidence led by the parties in the suit clearly shows that Abu Sufian and after him. his heirs are in possession of half of the lapd taken settlement by the Hukumnama and hence claim of title in.the entire land of Hukumnama by the plaintiffs is not sustainable in law, that High Court Division in the background of the evidence on record held both the plaintiffs and the defendants are in possession and title being in favour of Firoz alone the possession should be construed the possession of Firoz alone and Abu Sufian may be treated as "intruder" is not well founded in law since Abu Sufian as from the date of settlement i.e. from 1344 BS, possessed the land and the SA record was prepared in his name, as such, he cannot be considered intruder. The learned Counsel continues that Abu Sufian with, the consent of Firoz Bhuiyan spent money and, built huts in the land in suit and lived there and thereafter defendants are living and that as plaintiffs are in possession of half of the total land taken settlement by the Hukumnama the same implies That the plaintiffs are not in possession of the other half and, as such suit as framed seeking mere declaration of title is not maintainable. The learned Counsel further submits that Firoz Bhuiyan waved his right in respect of half of the land taken settlement by the Hukumnama by allowing Abu Sufian to possess half of the land of the total quantity of land taken settlement by the Hukumnama dated 10th Kartick, 1344 BS and thus Firoz Bhuiyan lost his right in half of the land taken settlement by the Hukumnama by waiver, estoppel and acquiescence. The learned Counsel lastly, submits that finding of the High Court Division that both parties are in possession was not challenged by the plaintiffs and, as such, the said finding alone is sufficient for the purpose of upholding the contention of the defendants that the suit as framed is not maintainable or, in other words, suit seeking mere declaration of title is not maintainable.

13. As against the aforesaid contentions of the learned Counsel of the appellants the learned Advocate, who appeared with the leave of the Court for the plaintiff respondents has submitted that the Court of first instance and the appellate Court having had found that the plaintiffs have right, title and possession in the land in suit, as such, the contention of the defendants that the suit as framed is barred by the provision of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act has no substance, that judgment of the High Court Division as well as of the Courts below being based on correct appreciation of the evidence on record and there being no infirmity in the judgment of the High Court Division the appeal is liable to be dismissed. It has also been submitted by the learned Advocate that the judgment of the Court of first instance and the lower appellate Court being not based on misreading of evidence and that the evidence of PWs 2 and 4 as in no way suggest that the defendants are in possession of the land in suit at the time of fling of the suit, as such, the contention of the defendants that they along with the plaintiffs are in possession of the land in suit merits no consideration. It has also been submitted by the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-respondents that subsequent to the filing of the suit plaintiffs were dispossessed from the land in suit and the said fact as has found place in the evidence of PW 1 it is not legally well founded to say that the suit framed is not maintainable. It has also been submitted by the learned Advocate that suggestion was made to the PW 1 as to joint possession of Firoz Bhuiyan and Abu Sufian and of having defendants' huts in the land in suit, but the same was denied by the said witness. The learned Advocate continues that although it was the case of the defendants that while the original owners expressed their intention to settle the land then Firoz Bhuiyan and Abu Sufian agreed to take settlement of the land and accordingly, from the income of the joint family salami was paid and the land in suit was taken settlement for the benefit of the two brothers but Firoz Bhuiyan in breach of trust took the settlement of the land in suit in his own name and later on Firoz Bhuiyan of his own got the SA record prepared in respect of the land taken settlement as well as the ancestral property in equal share, but the case so pleaded was not established by the defendants by leading reliable evidence. The learned Counsel also referred to the observation of the High Court Division that title of the land in suit is of Firoz Bhuiyan and that Abu Sufian and after him the defendants are "intruder" in the land in suit.

14. From the evidence on record as well as from findings of the High Court Division it is seen that defendants are in possession of the land in suit. PW 1 has also admitted possession of the defendant Nos. 1-9 in the land in suit. The High Court Division has considered the possession of the defendants as of "intruder".

15. The learned Counsel for the appellants has submitted that as from the evidence on record it is seen that the defendants are in possession of the land in suit and in that state of the matter the plaintiffs having had not asked for consequential relief, their suit in view of the provision of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act was not maintainable. In support of the aforesaid submission the learned Counsel has referred to the case of Munsur Ali Mallik vs Md Nurul Haque Mallik and others reported in 1986 BCR (AD) 56. Therein it has been observed that "institution of the suit for declaration simplicities when the plaintiff should have asked for consequential relief" renders a suit non-maintainable.

16. The fact of the reported case, in short, is that a suit was filed seeking declaration that the decree obtained in Title Suit No. 69 of 1961 is fraudulent, void, collusive, inoperative and not binding upon the plaintiff contending that in previous Title Suit Nos. 108 and 275 of 1958 the Court of Munsif declared his title to the land in suit and thereupon he mutated his name and is in possession of the land in suit, that he came to know of the decree obtained by Lakshman Chandra Dhupi, predecessor of the defendant in Title Suit No. 69 of 1961 in respect of the land in suit making false claim on the basis of settlement and obtained decree fraudulently by suppressing summons and showing false return of service and the said decree as has cast cloud in his title and hence the suit. The suit was decreed by the trial Court. On appeal decree of the trial Court was set aside and the suit was dismissed. The appellate Court reversed the decree of the trial Court on the view that as the defendant challenged possession of the plaintiff, it was necessary for the plaintiff to file a regular title suit for declaration of his title and confirmation of his possession in the disputed land and in that suit the plaintiff also could have challenged the legality of the impugned decree (decree in Title Suit No. 69 of 1961). The appellate Court, in the background of the aforesaid observation, took the view that the suit was barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and, as such, the suit was not maintainable. The plaintiff filed second appeal before the High Court Division and the High Court Division held that the suit was not maintainable in view of the provision of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act as the plaintiff did not pray for consequential relief which he could have asked for in the suit itself.  The second appeal was dismissed. Leave was granted to consider the contention whether the suit for declaration of title simplicities could .be maintained. It may be mentioned in Title Suit No. 69 of 1961, decree whereof was challenged by the plaintiff .he was not a party, in the said suit. This Court observed in the reported case that the learned Counsel for the appellant in support of the appeal relied on the, decrees obtained by plaintiff in Title Suit Nos.108 and 275 of 1958. In the judgment of the above referred case it has been observed "But when he was confronted with the later decree. that was obtained by the predecessor of the defendant in Title Suit No.69 of 1961 he found it difficult to justify in bringing a suit for declaration simpliciter when the plaintiff should have asked for consequential relief that was not done". This Court further observed, "In view of the clear proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act there is no hesitation in saying that without prayer for consequential relief such suit should not be maintained. The High Court Division and the appellate Court below have rightly dismissed the suit". This Court in the background of the aforesaid observations dismissed the appeal.

17. The learned Counsel for the appellants has also submitted that when the plaintiffs, as seen from the evidence on record are out of possession of the land in suit their suit for declaration of title simpliciter was not maintainable and the High Court Division itself having noticed that the defendants are in possession of the land in suit, although considered the possession of the defendants as of "intruder", the said Division was in serious error in discharging the Rule or, in other words, in not making the Rule absolute and thereupon in not dismissing the suit of the plaintiff. In support of his contention that when the plaintiff is out of possession of the land in suit his suit for mere declaration of title is not maintainable the learned Counsel has referred to the decision in the case of Dudu Mia and others vs Ekram Miah Chowdhury, and others reported in 54 DLR (AD) 7 wherein it has been observed "Plaintiff's suit was for mere declaration of title. Plaintiff having failed to prove his possession in the land in suit, in law the suit was not maintainable". The learned Counsel for the appellant has also submitted that Firoz Bhuiyan by waiver, estoppel and acquiescence lost his title in the land in suit since he allowed his full brother Abu Sufian to possess half of the land taken settlement by the Hukumnama of the year 1344 BS and to erect but and that SA record which was prepared during the lifetime of Firoz Bhuiyan was not taken exception by him. The learned Counsel for the purpose of showing what particular fact or circumstance constitutes waiver, estoppel and acquiescence has referred to the case of Akhlasur Rahman and others vs Safarullah and others reported in 42 DLR (AD) 189 wherein what waiver means or what constitutes waiver as to that there is a quotation from Halsbury's Laws of England, Third Edition, Volume 14, page 637 and the same is as follows:

"Waiver is the abandonment of a right, and is either express or implied from conduct. A person who is entitled to the benefit of a stipulation in a contract or of a statutory provision may waive it, and allow the contract or transaction to proceed as though the stipulation or provision did not exist. Waiver of this kind depends upon consent and the fact that the other party has acted upon it is sufficient consideration. Where the waiver is not express, it may be implied from conduct which is inconsistent with the continuance of the right. It seems that, in general, where one party has, by his words or conduct, made to the other a promise or assurance with was intended to affect the legal relations between them and to be acted on accordingly, then once the other party has taken him at his word and acted on it, the party who gave the promise or assurance cannot afterwards he allowed to revert to the previous legal relationship as if no such promise or assurance had been made by him, but he must accept their legal relations subject to the qualification which he himself has so introduced, even though it is not supported in point of law by any consideration"

In the reported case it has also been observed upon referring to page 638 of Halsbury's Laws of England, Third Edition, Volume 14 "it has been stated that "acquiescence" in its proper legal sense implies that a person abstains from interfering while a violation of his legal rights is in progress" and further that "Acquiescence operates by way of estoppel. It is acquiescence in such circumstances that assent may reasonably be inferred, and is an instance of estoppel by words or conduct. Consequently, if the whole circumstances are proper for raising this estoppel, the party acquiescing cannot afterwards complain of the violation of his right".

<u>18. The learned Counsel in support of his submission regarding estoppel on the part of Firoz Bhuiyan in allowing his brother Abu Sufian to enjoy the property by possessing and erecting but taken settlement by the Hukumnama of the year 1344 BS and of not taking any exception to the preparation of the SA record prepared during the lifetime of Firoz Bhuiyan has referred to the case of Hari Bhusan Halder vs Sheikh Abdul and others reported in AIR 1927 Calcutta 54 wherein it has been observed "That rule is, however, that where a person in bonfire belief that a certain property belongs to him spends money upon it and the true owner stands by and allows him to spend the money and make improvements upon his land, the true owner is stopped from asserting his title to the land as against the person making improvements in such benefice belief."</u>

<u>From the evidence of the PWs as well as the DWs it is seen that Firoz Bhuiyan and Abu Sufian possessed the property purchased by the Hukumnama of the year 1344 BS in equal share and in their respective share they erected huts and lived therein. It is seen from the evidence of PW 4 that the defendants have huts in the land in suit and it is also seen from the evidence of DW 4 that defendants have their huts in the land in suit and they are living therein. The aforesaid positive statement of the DW 4 in examination-in-chief was not challenged by the plaintiffs at the time of cross-examination of the witness.</u>

<u>19. In the afore state of the matter the contention made from the side of the appellants that as Firoz Bhuiyan waived his right in respect of half of the property taken settlement by the Hukumnama of the year 1344 BS and thus lost his right in the half of the property by waiver, estoppel and acquiescence appears to be of substance.</u>

<u>20. It is seen from the judgment of the High Court Division as well as the courts below that question of possession in the background of the evidence on record touching maintainability of the suit was not considered by the said Courts. The High Court Division although noticed from the materials on record that the plaintiffs and the defendants are in possession of the land in suit but considered the possession of the defendants as of "intruder" taking the view that title of the property in suit was of Firoz Bhuiyan. As stated hereinbefore that plaintiff No. 1, who figured as PW 1 has stated in his deposition that taking advantage of the wrong record the plaintiffs are in possession of the land in suit for the last one year. Other PWs have also stated that plaintiffs have their huts in the land in suit and it is seen from the evidence on record same were erected by Abu Sufian during lifetime of Firoz Bhuiyan. In that state of the matter the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-respondents tried to explain the possession of the defendants stated by PW 1 upon making submission that the defendants went into possession of the land in suit after institution of the suit. But there is no such case from the side of the plaintiffs. There is nothing on record wherefrom it can be seen that at any time plaintiffs complained that after institution of the suit defendants dispossessed them. In that view of the matter, the contention of the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-respondents that the defendants dispossessed plaintiffs after institution of the suit is of no merit. The High Court Division, in our view, was in error in discharging the Rule when it was noticed by the said Division that the defendants are in possession of the land in suit and thus making plaintiffs' suit maintainable in view of the provision of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. The learned Counsel in taking exception to the finding of the High Court Division that the defendants are "intruder" in the land in suit has submitted that there was no case like that from plaintiffs' side or, in other words, it was never the contention of the plaintiffs that the defendants are "intruder" in the land in suit rather it was the case of the plaintiffs that they are in possession of the land in suit. In the background of the said assertion, which is contrary, to the materials on record, framing the suit seeking mere declaration of title was wrong, submitted by the learned Counsel of the appellants. The learned Counsel also submits that the High Court Division failed to notice from the evidence on record that plaintiffs failed to prove their possession in the land in suit and consequent thereupon the suit was not maintainable without prayer for consequential relief. It has been submitted by the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-respondents that the finding as to fact of possession of the land in suit by the plaintiffs is concurrent one and, as such, the same cannot be reopened in the appeal from the side of the defendants.</u>

21. It has been submitted by the learned Counsel for the appellants, that particular finding even if concurrent but while same is not based on evidence or contrary to the evidence, the same is not immune from challenge and, as such, can very much be interfered by a revisional Court or, for that matter, in an appeal against the judgment of the revisional Court and in support of the aforesaid submission the learned Counsel has referred to the case of Moaher Sowdagar vs M Zahirul Alam reported in 40 DLR (AD) 62, wherein it has been observed "But in view of the facts discussed above we find that the very basis of the finding of the two courts below is a misconception as to which tenders are relevant in this suit. As such, the concurrent finding cannot claim any immunity".

22. In view of the discussions made herein-above we find merit in the appeal. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed with costs.

End.
